title: Ventricles of the brain (lateral)
attribution: 3D anatomy from Z-Anatomy, built on BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA). Rendered in Blender; surface detail added with an image model.

rows: Location

C-shaped cavity inside each cerebral hemisphere. It has a frontal (anterior) horn in the frontal lobe, a body in the parietal lobe, an occipital (posterior) horn in the occipital lobe and a temporal (inferior) horn in the temporal lobe.
Function
Holds cerebrospinal fluid, which leaves through the interventricular foramen (of Monro) into the third ventricle.
Contains
Choroid plexus, which makes cerebrospinal fluid, in the body and the temporal horn. The frontal and occipital horns have none.
hy: The head of the caudate nucleus bulges into the lateral wall of the frontal horn. In Huntington disease the caudate nucleus wastes away, so the frontal horns typically look enlarged on a brain scan.
Normal pressure hydrocephalus, usually in older people: the ventricles enlarge and classically cause urinary incontinence, an unsteady shuffling gait and dementia (wet, wobbly and wacky).

rows: Location
Narrow, slit-like cavity in the midline of the diencephalon, between the right and left thalamus and hypothalamus.
Function
Receives cerebrospinal fluid from each lateral ventricle through the interventricular foramen (of Monro) and passes it through the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle.
Features

The thalamus above and the hypothalamus below form each side wall. Choroid plexus hangs from its roof, and in most brains the interthalamic adhesion crosses it. Its floor dips into the stalk of the pituitary gland.
hy: A colloid cyst at the front of its roof can block the interventricular foramina and cause hydrocephalus of both lateral ventricles, with headaches that may come on suddenly or change with the position of the head.

rows: Location
Narrow channel through the midbrain, between the tectum (the colliculi) behind and the tegmentum in front. The periaqueductal gray matter surrounds it.
Function
Carries cerebrospinal fluid from the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle. It has no choroid plexus.
hy: Aqueduct stenosis is a common cause of congenital obstructive (noncommunicating) hydrocephalus. The aqueduct is the narrowest part of the ventricular system, and when it is blocked the lateral and third ventricles enlarge while the fourth does not.
A tumor of the pineal region can press on the aqueduct, causing hydrocephalus, and on the nearby tectum, causing paralysis of upward gaze (Parinaud syndrome).

rows: Location
Tent-shaped cavity of the hindbrain, with the pons and the upper medulla in front and the cerebellum behind. Its diamond-shaped floor is the rhomboid fossa.
Function
Receives cerebrospinal fluid from the cerebral aqueduct and lets it out into the subarachnoid space. Below, it narrows into the central canal of the medulla and spinal cord.
Features

Three openings lead to the subarachnoid space: one median aperture (foramen of Magendie) in the lower part of the roof and two lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka) at the ends of the lateral recesses. Choroid plexus lies in the lower part of the roof.
hy: Posterior fossa tumors of childhood, such as medulloblastoma and ependymoma, can compress or fill the fourth ventricle and cause obstructive hydrocephalus.
Dandy-Walker malformation: the cerebellar vermis is absent or very small and the fourth ventricle is enlarged into a cyst that fills the posterior fossa, often with hydrocephalus.
